newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia allows diamond exports up to end of May - ARS.
newsitem.headline: Russia allows diamond exports up to end of May - ARS.

text.p: The Russian government has signed a decree on diamond export quotas which will free up exports until the end of May, a senior official at Russia's main diamond producer Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS) said on Wednesday.
"It is true that the government has signed the decree allowing us to export up until the end of May," Lev Safonov, first vice president of ARS, told Reuters.
He added that a long-delayed gem trade deal with South African giant De Beers had not been signed, but that he hoped President Boris Yeltsin would give final approval for the deal in May or June.
"The decree on exports may help that process," he said.
In a separate development, a Moscow-based De Beers official said the firm was looking to jointly develop a diamond mine with Russia's Severalmaz, a company based in the northern city of Arkhangelsk.
Safonov said that De Beers would also be allowed to export gems from Russia up until the end of this month under the decree, which ARS officials said was signed late in April.
"De Beers will also be able to export gems thay have bought from us so far this year," he said.
De Beers bought diamonds from ARS during the first four months of 1997, but had been unable to export them because no diamond export quota decree had been signed.

The South African company sharply curtailed its purchases of Russian diamonds at the end of last year, because Moscow failed to communicate its position on a draft trade agreement submitted to the government in October 1996.
Both ARS and De Beers are keen for the deal to go through, but have been frustrated by the government's failure to deal with the issue.

ARS officials said in mid-April that First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais had made assurances the deal would be signed no later than May 1. But as yet there has been no news on the fate of the deal, they said on Wednesday.

De Beers' London-based Central Selling Organisation controls about three quarters of the world's $4.5 billion-a-year trade in uncut diamonds, and Russian typically accounts for about 20 percent of annual CSO sales.
A mining official at De Beers' Moscow office said the firm was looking to help develop a mine in the Arkhangelsk region, and that other diamond mining firms had also shown interest.
"We have put forward in our proposal that we would be looking for a 50 percent stake (in Severalmaz)," he said.

The official added that detailed work on the project had not been carried out, and declined to comment on estimates reported by the Itar-Tass agency, quoting Russian experts, that the project could cost $700 million.
"We haven't been able to do a lot of detailed work on the deposit, or what the project would cost," he said.
